title: Troubleshooting Guide
text:
TipIn this section




Diagnosing convergence problems
Fixing energy drift and NaN values
Resolving performance bottlenecks
Common pitfalls and their solutions





When a simulation fails or produces unexpected results, systematic diagnosis is essential:

Check energy conservation — does TotEng drift? Is PotEng stable?
Check forces — are any atoms experiencing huge forces?
Check charges — are electrode charges oscillating wildly?
Check geometry — are atoms overlapping? Are regions correct?






Electrode charges oscillate wildly between timesteps (e.g., ±10 e on one electrode per step).



Cause
Solution




eta too small
Increase eta (try 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 Å⁻¹)


eta too large
Decrease eta (try 0.5, 0.3 Å⁻¹)


Timestep too large
Reduce dt to 0.5 fs


Overlapping atoms
Run minimization before dynamics


Tolerance too tight
Use kspace_style pppm 1e-4






NaN or Inf appears in PotEng, Temp, or other quantities.



Cause
Solution




Atoms overlapping
Minimize before dynamics; check pair_coeff


Bonds too stretched
Use fix shake to constrain; reduce timestep


Kspace tolerance
Use looser tolerance (1e-4)


Electrode too close
Increase electrode separation


eta too small
Increase eta for better matrix conditioning






ERROR: Fix electrode: matrix inversion failed



Cause
Solution




Singular matrix
Increase eta; check for overlapping atoms


Too many electrode atoms
Use algo mat_cg or algo cg


Geometric issue
Verify electrode geometry is valid






PPPM cannot achieve requested tolerance.



Cause
Solution




Too many close contacts
Minimize; separate overlapping atoms


Box too anisotropic
Adjust kspace parameters


Tolerance too tight
Use 1e-4 instead of 1e-5









Total energy increases or decreases monotonically over time.



Cause
Solution




Timestep too large
Reduce dt (try 0.5 fs, 1 fs)


Cutoff too small
Increase cutoff (12 Å for water)


Thermostat conflict
Remove one thermostat


Force spike
Minimize before running



Check energy conservation:
# Run NVE for 10 ps
fix conservative all nve
run 10000    # 10 ps at 1 fs

# In output, check TotEng drift
# Acceptable: < 0.1% over 10 ps



PotEng goes to large negative or positive values.



Cause
Solution




Atoms too close
Minimize; check pair_coeff (epsilon too large)


Electrode atoms too close to electrolyte
Increase LJ repulsion


Bonds over-stretched
Use fix shake; reduce timestep






Temp is far from target even with thermostat.







Cause
Solution




Damping time wrong
For Langevin, 100.0 is reasonable; try 50.0 or 200.0


Thermostat on frozen atoms
Only thermostat mobile atoms


Initial velocities too hot/cold
Use velocity all create 300.0 12345 before dynamics









# Print atom positions near problematic region
dump debug all custom 1 debug.xyz id type x y z

# Check which atoms are in which group
group bot print

# Check box dimensions
print "Box: $(xhi) $(yhi) $(zhi)"

# Check for overlapping regions
region bot check overlap



Common when creating atoms in overlapping regions.
# Don't do this:
region bot block 0 20 0 20 0 10
create_atoms 1 region bot
region top block 0 20 0 20 0 10    # OVERLAPS with bot
create_atoms 2 region top
Fix: Ensure regions don’t overlap.



# Correct: regions cover full box height with gap for electrolyte
region box block 0 20 0 20 0 60
region bot block 0 20 0 20 0 5
region top block 0 20 0 20 55 60
region elyte block 0 20 0 20 5 55    # Gap between 5 and 55






ERROR: kspace style pppm is not supported with fix electrode
Cause: Standard pppm doesn’t provide electrode interaction matrices.
Fix:
kspace_style pppm/electrode 1e-5    # Electrode-aware version



ERROR: Fix electrode group has no atoms
Cause: Group name doesn’t exist or has no atoms.
Fix:
group bot region bot    # Define group BEFORE fix
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp ...



Electrode potentials are always in volts regardless of units setting.
units metal    # eV, but potential is still in VOLTS, not eV
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805    # -1.0 V, not -1.0 eV






If electrode charges take too long to equilibrate:







Cause
Solution




Matrix too large
Use algo mat_cg instead of mat_inv


Tolerance too tight
Loosen kspace tolerance


Too many electrode atoms
Reduce electrode thickness (3-4 Å sufficient)

title: The ELECTRODE Package
text:
TipIn this section




Three fix styles: electrode/conp, electrode/conq, electrode/thermo
Complete syntax reference with all options
Algorithm choices and when to use each
Kspace compatibility requirements and slab modifications
Output interpretation with concrete examples
Complete working input script template





The ELECTRODE package implements constant potential, constant charge, and thermopotentiostat methods for electrode-electrolyte simulations. It was developed by Ahrens-Iwers, Tee, and Meissner and first released in LAMMPS 4May2022.
Key capabilities: - Enforce fixed electrostatic potential on electrode groups - Compute induced charges as function of geometry and electrolyte - Track fluctuating potentials in constant charge mode - Model thermal fluctuations (Johnson-Nyquist noise) in electrochemistry
Requirements: - KSPACE package (must be enabled) - LAPACK and BLAS (or -D USE_INTERNAL_LINALG=yes with CMake)





cmake -B build -S . \
  -D PKG_ELECTRODE=yes \
  -D PKG_KSPACE=yes \
  -D USE_INTERNAL_LINALG=yes
cmake --build build
Note: The ELECTRODE package requires the KSPACE package to be enabled as well, because it relies on the kspace solvers for the electrode-electrode and electrode-electrolyte interaction matrices.



lmp -h | grep electrode
Should show ELECTRODE in the list of installed packages.






Purpose: Hold the electrostatic potential on each electrode group fixed; charges fluctuate to maintain the constraint.
Physical meaning: Models a potentiostat — the voltage is controlled, charge is the response. This is what you want for comparing to electrochemical experiments.
Syntax:
fix fxconp groupName electrode/conp potential eta keyword value ...








Argument
Description
Typical Values




groupName
Electrode group to constrain
Must exist before fix


potential
Electrode potential in volts
-2.0 to +2.0 V typical


eta
Gaussian smearing width (Å⁻¹)
1.0–2.0 (real) or 0.2–0.5 (metal)



Complete example:
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 couple top 1.0 symm on
Keywords:








Keyword
Description
Values




couple
Add additional electrode at specified potential
groupName V


symm
Enforce total electrode charge neutrality
on or off


algo
Solver algorithm
mat_inv, mat_cg, cg


etypes
Use type-based neighbor lists
on or off


ffield
Finite-field mode (periodic z)
on or off


write_mat
Write capacitance matrix to file
filename


read_mat
Read capacitance matrix from file
filename


write_inv
Write elastance matrix to file
filename


read_inv
Read elastance matrix from file
filename





Any equal-style variable can be used for potential. This enables:
Linear sweep (cyclic voltammetry-like):
variable V equal ramp(-1.0, 1.0)
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp v_V 1.805 couple top 1.0
Sinusoidal (AC perturbation):
variable V equal "2.0 * sin(time * 0.01)"
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp v_V 1.805
Stepped potential:
variable V equal 0.5
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp v_V 1.805 couple top -0.5
run 10000
variable V equal 1.0
run 10000




Purpose: Set the total charge on each electrode group; potentials fluctuate.
Physical meaning: Models a galvanostat — charge injection/extraction is controlled, voltage is the response. Use when you know the charge dynamics rather than voltage.
Syntax:
fix fxconq groupName electrode/conq charge eta keyword value ...








Argument
Description
Notes




groupName
Electrode group to constrain
Must exist before fix


charge
Total charge on electrode group
In units consistent with units setting


eta
Gaussian smearing width
Same units as conp



Complete example:
fix fxconq bot electrode/conq -0.5 1.805 couple top 0.5 symm on
Output: The vector component f_fxconq[2], f_fxconq[3], etc. gives the actual potential on each electrode — can be monitored to compute voltage response.
Accessing potentials:
variable V_bot equal f_fxconq[2]
variable V_top equal f_fxconq[3]
fix print all print 100 "V_bot = $(v_V_bot), V_top = $(v_V_top)"



Purpose: Add thermal fluctuations (Johnson-Nyquist noise) to both potential and charge.
Physical meaning: Models the thermodynamic consistency of charge/potential fluctuations. Essential for fluctuation-dissipation studies, non-equilibrium dynamics, and realistic finite-temperature electrode behavior.
Syntax:
fix fxthermo groupName electrode/thermo potential eta temp seed tau_v keyword value ...



Argument
Description
Notes




groupName
Electrode group
Must exist


potential
Mean potential
Fluctuates around this


eta
Gaussian smearing
Same as other fixes


temp
Temperature (K)
For thermal noise amplitude


seed
Random seed
Must be set for reproducibility


tau_v
Potential relaxation time
~50 fs typical



Complete example:
fix fxthermo bot electrode/thermo -1.0 1.805 300.0 12345 50.0 symm on
Physical basis: The fluctuation-dissipation theorem relates thermal noise to dissipative properties. For electrochemistry, the thermopotentiostat adds fluctuations to both potential and charge with correct statistics. This is important for: - Understanding noise in electrochemical sensors - Modeling electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) - Studying thermal effects on charging dynamics




The algo keyword controls how the capacitance/elastance problem is solved:



Algorithm
Precomputation
Memory
Speed
Electrode Motion




mat_inv
Capacitance matrix C (N²)
High
Fast
Static only


mat_cg
Elastance matrix S (N²)
Medium
Medium
Static only


cg
None
Low
Slowest
Allowed



Where N = number of electrode groups (not atoms). For two electrodes (bot, top), N=2.


How it works: 1. At startup: compute capacitance matrix C and store it 2. At each step: solve q = C · V directly (matrix-vector multiply)
Trade-offs: - Fast per step (just multiplication) - High memory (stores N×N matrix) - Electrodes must remain fixed (matrix is geometry-specific) - If electrodes move, matrix becomes invalid
When to use: < 10,000 electrode atoms, static electrodes, need fastest per-step performance
Memory estimate: For N_electrode_groups = 2, matrix is 2×2 = trivial. For N = 100 (complex geometry), matrix is 100×100 = 40 KB. For N = 10,000, matrix is 10000×10000 = 800 MB.



How it works: 1. At startup: compute and store elastance matrix S (inverse of C) 2. At each step: solve S · q = V via conjugate gradient (iterative)
Trade-offs: - Medium memory (same matrix size as mat_inv, but stored differently) - Slower per step (iterative solver) - Can handle slightly larger systems - Still requires fixed electrodes
When to use: Medium systems where memory matters; limited electrode motion



How it works: 1. No precomputation 2. At each step: solve full A · q = b via conjugate gradient
Trade-offs: - Slowest per step (full iterative solve every step) - Lowest memory (no matrix storage) - Required for moving electrodes (charging/discharging dynamics)
When to use: Electrodes move significantly; very large electrode systems where memory is limiting



# Small static system → mat_inv (fastest)
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 algo mat_inv

# Medium static system → mat_cg (balanced)
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 algo mat_cg

# Dynamic electrodes → cg (only option)
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 algo cg






ELECTRODE requires electrode-aware kspace styles that provide: 1. Electrode-electrode interaction matrix 2. Electrode-electrolyte interaction vector
Standard ewald or pppm will not work — they lack the electrode interaction matrices.



kspace_style ewald/electrode 1e-5
kspace_style pppm/electrode 1e-5
kspace_style pppm/electrode/intel 1e-5    # Intel-optimized
Note: You cannot combine standard pppm with ELECTRODE fixes. You must use pppm/electrode.



kspace_modify slab 3          # 2D Ewald correction (non-periodic z)
kspace_modify one-step        # faster elastance computation; less accurate
kspace_modify force 1e-4     # override tolerance for kspace only
kspace_modify order 5        # PPPM interpolation order (higher = more accurate)














Option
Description
Values




algo
Solver algorithm
mat_inv, mat_cg, cg


symm
Charge neutrality
on, off


ffield
Finite-field mode
on, off


etypes
Type-based neighbor lists
on, off


couple
Additional electrode group
groupName V or groupName Q






For capacitor-like systems with two electrodes:
symm on    # Total electrode charge = 0 (system is neutral)
With symm on: - electrode/conp: if bot = -1 V, top automatically adjusts to maintain symm - electrode/conq: if bot = -0.5 e/atom, top = +0.5 e/atom
For asymmetric systems or single electrodes:
symm off    # No charge neutrality constraint



fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 couple top 1.0 ffield on symm on
What it does: - Uses periodic boundary in z (not slab geometry) - Potential difference applied via internal E-field: \(E = V / d\) - No vacuum region needed - Smaller z-dimension possible (saves atoms)
Requirements: - Must use boundary p p p (fully periodic) - Requires symm on (total charge neutrality)
When to use: You want smaller cells; better for some geometries; want infinite stack model; no surface effects needed



Since LAMMPS restart files don’t yet save ELECTRODE state, use matrix I/O for restart:
# Save during run
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 write_inv 1000 filename.elast

# Load at startup
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 read_inv filename.elast
Why this matters: Without matrix I/O, you must recompute the matrix from scratch on restart, which can be slow for large electrode systems.



For real metal response (quantum corrections to simple dielectric):
fix_modify fxconp tf 0.001    # Thomas-Fermi screening length (Å)
Physical effect: Adds metallic screening beyond the simple dielectric model. The screening length λ_TF characterizes how charges distribute in a real metal.
When to use: Electrode is a real metal (Au, Pt, Ag) and quantum effects matter for your application.






f_ID — scalar: the energy added to the system by the fix.
For constant potential: -Σ q_i V_i (work done by electrodes on the system)
Check this for energy conservation (should be small fluctuations around constant in NVE).



For electrode/conp:



Index
Meaning




f_ID[1]
Energy (same as scalar)


f_ID[2]
Potential on electrode 1 (should match specified)


f_ID[3]
Potential on electrode 2 (if couple used)


…
…



For electrode/conq:



Index
Meaning




f_ID[1]
Energy


f_ID[2]
Potential on electrode 1 (fluctuates!)


f_ID[3]
Potential on electrode 2


…
…






f_ID[4] through f_ID[4+N] — rows of the capacitance matrix.
For a two-electrode system:
f_ID[4] = C_11 (charge response of electrode 1 to electrode 1 potential)
f_ID[5] = C_12 (charge response of electrode 1 to electrode 2 potential)
f_ID[6] = C_21 (charge response of electrode 2 to electrode 1 potential)
f_ID[7] = C_22 (charge response of electrode 2 to electrode 2 potential)



# For conp fix named fxconp
variable Q_bot equal f_fxconp[5]    # bottom electrode charge
variable Q_top equal f_fxconp[6]    # top electrode charge
variable E_elec equal f_fxconp[1]   # electrode work term

# For conq fix named fxconq
variable V_bot equal f_fxconq[2]    # bottom electrode potential
variable V_top equal f_fxconq[3]    # top electrode potential

# Print during run
fix printQ all print 100 "Q_bot = $(v_Q_bot) Q_top = $(v_Q_top)"




# ============================================
# Constant Potential Supercapacitor
# Au electrodes, SPC/E water, 1M NaCl
# ============================================

units metal
atom_style charge
boundary p p f

# --- Box and geometry ---
variable Lx equal 20
variable Ly equal 20
variable Lz equal 60

region box block 0 $Lx 0 $Ly 0 $Lz
create_box 5 box    # 1=bot electrode, 2=top, 3=O, 4=H, 5=Na, 6=Cl

region bot block 0 $Lx 0 $Ly 0 5
region top block 0 $Lx 0 $Ly 55 $Lz
region elyte block 0 $Lx 0 $Ly 5 55

create_atoms 1 region bot    # bottom electrode
create_atoms 2 region top    # top electrode
# (Water and ions added separately - use moltemplate or similar)

group bot region bot
group top region top
group elyte region elyte
group electrode union bot top

# --- Force field ---
pair_style lj/cut/coul/long 10.0

# Electrode-electrode (soft repulsion)
pair_coeff 1 1 0.01 3.0
pair_coeff 2 2 0.01 3.0
pair_coeff 1 2 0.005 3.0

# Water LJ (SPC/E)
pair_coeff 3 3 0.155 3.166    # O
pair_coeff 4 4 0.0 0.0        # H

# Ion LJ
pair_coeff 5 5 0.0874 3.40    # Na
pair_coeff 6 6 0.100 4.45     # Cl

# Cross terms
pair_coeff 1 3 0.005 3.1
pair_coeff 2 3 0.005 3.1
pair_coeff 1 4 0.0 0.0
pair_coeff 2 4 0.0 0.0
pair_coeff 5 3 0.114 3.28    # Na-O
pair_coeff 6 3 0.124 3.81    # Cl-O
# ... all other cross terms needed ...

kspace_style pppm/electrode 1e-5
kspace_modify slab 3

# --- ELECTRODE fix ---
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 couple top 1.0 symm on

# --- Integrators ---
fix frozen all nve           # frozen electrodes
fix mytemp elyte langevin 300.0 300.0 100.0 12345

# --- Output ---
thermo 100
thermo_style custom step temp pe ke vol density f_fxconp[1]

variable Q_bot equal f_fxconp[5]
variable Q_top equal f_fxconp[6]
fix printQ all print 100 "Q_bot = $(v_Q_bot) Q_top = $(v_Q_top)"

dump 1 all custom 100 traj.lammpstrj id type x y z q

# --- Run ---
minimize 1e-6 1e-9 1000 10000
run 10000

Cause
Solution

eta too small or too large
Try eta = 1.0 or 2.0 (real units)


Matrix inversion fails
Singular matrix
Increase eta or check geometry

Overlapping atoms
Minimize before dynamics


Slow performance
Large matrix storage

title: The ELECTRODE Package
text:
The ELECTRODE package implements constant potential, constant charge, and thermopotentiostat methods for electrode-electrolyte simulations. It was developed by Ahrens-Iwers, Tee, and Meissner and first released in LAMMPS 4May2022.
Key capabilities: - Enforce fixed electrostatic potential on electrode groups - Compute induced charges as function of geometry and electrolyte - Track fluctuating potentials in constant charge mode - Model thermal fluctuations (Johnson-Nyquist noise) in electrochemistry
Requirements: - KSPACE package (must be enabled) - LAPACK and BLAS (or -D USE_INTERNAL_LINALG=yes with CMake)

  -D PKG_KSPACE=yes \

cmake --build build

The algo keyword controls how the capacitance/elastance problem is solved:



Algorithm

Where N = number of electrode groups (not atoms). For two electrodes (bot, top), N=2.


How it works: 1. At startup: compute capacitance matrix C and store it 2. At each step: solve q = C · V directly (matrix-vector multiply)
Trade-offs: - Fast per step (just multiplication) - High memory (stores N×N matrix) - Electrodes must remain fixed (matrix is geometry-specific) - If electrodes move, matrix becomes invalid
When to use: < 10,000 electrode atoms, static electrodes, need fastest per-step performance
Memory estimate: For N_electrode_groups = 2, matrix is 2×2 = trivial. For N = 100 (complex geometry), matrix is 100×100 = 40 KB. For N = 10,000, matrix is 10000×10000 = 800 MB.



How it works: 1. At startup: compute and store elastance matrix S (inverse of C) 2. At each step: solve S · q = V via conjugate gradient (iterative)
Trade-offs: - Medium memory (same matrix size as mat_inv, but stored differently) - Slower per step (iterative solver) - Can handle slightly larger systems - Still requires fixed electrodes
When to use: Medium systems where memory matters; limited electrode motion



How it works: 1. No precomputation 2. At each step: solve full A · q = b via conjugate gradient
Trade-offs: - Slowest per step (full iterative solve every step) - Lowest memory (no matrix storage) - Required for moving electrodes (charging/discharging dynamics)
When to use: Electrodes move significantly; very large electrode systems where memory is limiting

fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 algo mat_inv

# Medium static system → mat_cg (balanced)
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 algo mat_cg

# Dynamic electrodes → cg (only option)
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 algo cg

variable Ly equal 20
variable Lz equal 60

title: Electrostatics
text:
TipIn this section




Why long-range Coulomb is computationally hard
How Ewald summation splits the problem conceptually
How PPPM achieves O(N log N) scaling
Why slab geometry needs special treatment
Pair-kspace consistency rules
Practical guidance on choosing tolerance and debugging





Electrostatic interactions are long-range:
\[V(r) = k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r}\]
Unlike LJ (which decays as r⁻⁶), Coulomb falls off slowly. In a periodic system, the sum of all pairwise Coulomb interactions does not converge quickly — you cannot simply cut it off at a reasonable distance without introducing large errors.



Direct summation
Cost
Problem




All pairs (N²/2)
O(N²)
Prohibitive for large N


Cutoff at 10 Å
O(N)
~10–50% error for ionic systems



The challenge: we need the long-range part of Coulomb for accuracy, but we cannot sum it directly because there are too many pairs.
Why Coulomb is harder than LJ: - For unit charges at 3 Å: V ≈ 110 kcal/mol (real units) - For LJ minimum at same distance: V ≈ -1 kcal/mol - Coulomb is 100× larger and decays slower





Ewald summation splits the Coulomb sum into three parts:
\[V_{Coul} = V_{real} + V_{recip} + V_{self}\]








Term
Description
How It’s Computed




Real space
Short-range Coulomb (direct sum)
Cutoff-based; fast for small r


Reciprocal space
Long-range (Fourier transform)
FFT-based; fast for large N


Self term
Corrects for double-counting
Analytic formula







Smear each charge into a Gaussian cloud (width determined by α)
Real space: interaction of Gaussians with original charges (short-range, convergent)
Reciprocal space: interaction of Gaussians with each other in Fourier space (long-range, also convergent)
Self term: subtract the interaction of each charge with its own Gaussian




The problem with direct Coulomb sum is that \(1/r\) is slowly decaying. By smearing charges into Gaussians:

The short-range interaction (original charge × Gaussian of neighbor) converges quickly
The long-range interaction (Gaussian × Gaussian) becomes smooth and amenable to Fourier methods

The Ewald parameter α controls the split: - Large α: Gaussian is narrow → real-space converges fast → reciprocal space slow - Small α: Gaussian is wide → real-space converges slow → reciprocal space fast
For typical systems, α ≈ 0.2–0.5 Å⁻¹ (real units). LAMMPS chooses a reasonable default based on the system size and cutoff.



kspace_style ewald 1e-5
1e-5 = desired RMS force accuracy (relative to force magnitude). Tighter tolerance = more accurate = slower.
How to interpret tolerance: If the RMS force on atoms is ~100 kcal/mol/Å, a tolerance of 1e-5 means the kspace force error is ~0.001 kcal/mol/Å (negligible).






Ewald scales as O(N³/²). For very large systems, this is still prohibitive.
PPPM (Particle-Particle Particle-Mesh, also called PME — Particle Mesh Ewald) maps charges to a regular mesh and uses FFT for the reciprocal space sum:
\[O(N \log N) \text{ scaling}\]




Distribute charges to mesh: each charge assigned to nearby mesh points (Gaussian or cloud-in-cell scheme)
FFT to reciprocal space: ρ(r) → ρ(k) (charge density in k-space)
Multiply by Green’s function: apply the Coulomb kernel \(4π/k²\) in k-space
FFT back to real space: get the long-range potential on the mesh
Interpolate forces to particles: mesh → atom forces via shape function

The key insight: convolution with Green’s function becomes multiplication in Fourier space. FFT does this efficiently.



kspace_style pppm 1e-5
For ELECTRODE systems, use the electrode-aware variant:
kspace_style pppm/electrode 1e-5






Tolerance
Force RMS Error
Relative Error
Speed




1e-3
~1%
Large
Fastest


1e-4
~0.1%
Noticeable
Fast

~0.01%
Usually fine
Medium

~0.001%
Precise

For production: 1e-5 is standard. For precise energy calculations (e.g., comparing binding energies): 1e-6.






pair_style lj/cut/coul/cut 10.0   # real-space only; no kspace
kspace_style none                   # explicitly no long-range
DO NOT use for charged systems or electrolytes. The long-range part is significant — cutting it off introduces errors of 10–50%.




Neutral, sparse systems (gases at low pressure)
Very short simulations where speed matters more than accuracy
Testing/debugging before production
Systems with all charges screened by high dielectric (but even then, be careful)




For 1M NaCl solution: - Bulk screening length ≈ 10 Å - But at electrode surfaces, unscreened charges persist - Cutting off at 10 Å means you miss the long-range surface interactions entirely - This changes capacitance by 20–50%
Conclusion: for electrode-electrolyte simulations, always use PPPM.






With boundary p p p, the system is a periodic tile repeating infinitely. Ewald/PPPM works straightforwardly.



For electrode-electrolyte simulations:
boundary p p f    # non-periodic z
The z-direction has a vacuum gap. This creates two electrode surfaces exposed to vacuum (or vacuum region above electrolyte).
Problem with slab geometry: electrostatics in 2D is different from 3D. The naive Ewald/PPPM sum would include artificial dipole-dipole interactions between periodic images in z.
Why this matters: Without correction, the computed electrostatic energy depends on how many times you replicate the cell in z — clearly wrong for a single interface.
Solution: 2D Ewald / slab correction
kspace_modify slab 3
This applies a correction for the slab geometry: - Assumes the system is infinitely periodic in x, y - Assumes finite (non-periodic) in z - Adds a dipole correction term that accounts for the missing images
The number 3 refers to the dimensionality being treated as 2D (slab). LAMMPS automatically handles the correction.






WarningForgot kspace_modify slab?



If you use boundary p p f without kspace_modify slab, you will get: - Artificially high pressure in z-direction - Incorrect forces on atoms near the surface - Wrong double-layer structure and capacitance
Always add kspace_modify slab 3 (or equivalent) for non-periodic z.





The slab correction adds a term that accounts for the net dipole moment of the slab interacting with its periodic images. It has the form:
\[V_{dipole} = \frac{2\pi}{V} \left|\sum_i q_i z_i\right|^2\]
Where the sum is over all charges in the cell. This term is added to the reciprocal-space energy.
Physical interpretation: a polar slab has a dipole moment. In 3D periodic boundaries, that dipole would interact with infinitely many images. In slab geometry, only the x,y periodicity remains, and the correction accounts for the missing z-interactions.



boundary p p p    # fully periodic
# In fix electrode/conp:
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 couple top 1.0 ffield on
With ffield on, the system is treated as an infinite stack of identical cells: - No vacuum region needed - Smaller z-dimension possible (saves atoms) - Requires symm on (total charge neutrality) - Uses internal E-field to apply potential difference: \(E = V/d\)
Advantages: - Better scaling for large systems (fully periodic) - No slab correction needed - Smaller cell means fewer atoms
Disadvantages: - Electrodes must be symmetric (infinite stack assumption) - Can’t model single-surface experiments - Requires careful treatment of dipole moment






The pair style determines what forces are computed in real space. The kspace style handles the long-range correction.
If you use coul/long or coul/long as part of a pair style, LAMMPS requires an appropriate kspace style. The long suffix means “long-range handled by kspace”.









Pair Style
Real Space
Kspace Style
Notes

LJ + Coulomb (short-range)
pppm or ewald
Standard for electrolytes


lj/cut/coul/cut
LJ + Coulomb (truncated)

Large error; only for testing


coul/long only
Coulomb (short-range only)
pppm or ewald
No LJ

LJ only

No electrostatics






If you use lj/cut/coul/long but no kspace style:
ERROR: Kspace style required for coul/long pair style
LAMMPS will error. You must add kspace.
If you use lj/cut/coul/cut but kspace_style pppm:
The truncated Coulomb in real space already includes some long-range contribution. Adding PPPM double-counts or produces wrong results. LAMMPS may warn but will likely compute nonsense.
Always match pair style to kspace style: coul/long → pppm/ewald; coul/cut → none.



For ELECTRODE simulations, you MUST use electrode-aware kspace styles:
kspace_style pppm/electrode 1e-5
kspace_style ewald/electrode 1e-5
These variants: - Provide electrode-electrode interaction matrix to the ELECTRODE fix - Handle the induced-charge electrostatics correctly (electrode charges are not fixed) - Are compatible with electrode/conp, electrode/conq, electrode/thermo
Standard pppm or ewald will error with ELECTRODE fixes.




kspace_modify slab 3              # 2D Ewald for non-periodic z (default = 3)
kspace_modify wire                 # wire boundary conditions
kspace_modify one-step            # faster but less accurate elastance matrix
kspace_modify force 1e-4          # override tolerance
kspace_modify order 5             # PPPM grid order (higher = more accurate but slower)

When to Use

2D Ewald correction
Non-periodic z (slab geometry)

Wire boundary conditions
Cylindrical geometry


one-step
Faster elastance matrix calculation
Large electrode systems; less accuracy needed


force
Override tolerance
When you want different accuracy than global setting


order
PPPM interpolation order
Higher = more accurate but slower (default = 5)








In thermodynamic output:
Kspace = 0.5 * Σ_k G(k) * |ρ(k)|²
KspaceEng = reciprocal-space energy contribution.
Large KspaceEng (relative to PairEng) indicates: - Many charged particles - Weak screening - Strong long-range interactions
For pure water at 1 g/cm³, KspaceEng is typically ~30% of PairEng. For ionic solutions, it can be 50%+.



With PPPM, energy is not strictly conserved (unlike NVE with exact Ewald). But drift should be small:

run 10000
# Check TotEng drift over this run
Drift > 0.1% over 10 ps indicates a problem (timestep, tolerance, overlapping atoms).

Reciprocal space: interaction of Gaussians with each other in Fourier space (long-range, also convergent)
Self term: subtract the interaction of each charge with its own Gaussian




The problem with direct Coulomb sum is that \(1/r\) is slowly decaying. By smearing charges into Gaussians:

The short-range interaction (original charge × Gaussian of neighbor) converges quickly
The long-range interaction (Gaussian × Gaussian) becomes smooth and amenable to Fourier methods

The Ewald parameter α controls the split: - Large α: Gaussian is narrow → real-space converges fast → reciprocal space slow - Small α: Gaussian is wide → real-space converges slow → reciprocal space fast
For typical systems, α ≈ 0.2–0.5 Å⁻¹ (real units). LAMMPS chooses a reasonable default based on the system size and cutoff.



kspace_style ewald 1e-5
1e-5 = desired RMS force accuracy (relative to force magnitude). Tighter tolerance = more accurate = slower.
How to interpret tolerance: If the RMS force on atoms is ~100 kcal/mol/Å, a tolerance of 1e-5 means the kspace force error is ~0.001 kcal/mol/Å (negligible).

title: Electrostatics
text:
Ewald scales as O(N³/²). For very large systems, this is still prohibitive.
PPPM (Particle-Particle Particle-Mesh, also called PME — Particle Mesh Ewald) maps charges to a regular mesh and uses FFT for the reciprocal space sum:
\[O(N \log N) \text{ scaling}\]




Distribute charges to mesh: each charge assigned to nearby mesh points (Gaussian or cloud-in-cell scheme)
FFT to reciprocal space: ρ(r) → ρ(k) (charge density in k-space)
Multiply by Green’s function: apply the Coulomb kernel \(4π/k²\) in k-space
FFT back to real space: get the long-range potential on the mesh
Interpolate forces to particles: mesh → atom forces via shape function

The key insight: convolution with Green’s function becomes multiplication in Fourier space. FFT does this efficiently.



kspace_style pppm 1e-5
For ELECTRODE systems, use the electrode-aware variant:
kspace_style pppm/electrode 1e-5

Testing/debugging before production

For 1M NaCl solution: - Bulk screening length ≈ 10 Å - But at electrode surfaces, unscreened charges persist - Cutting off at 10 Å means you miss the long-range surface interactions entirely - This changes capacitance by 20–50%
Conclusion: for electrode-electrolyte simulations, always use PPPM.

title: Electrostatics
text:
With boundary p p p, the system is a periodic tile repeating infinitely. Ewald/PPPM works straightforwardly.



For electrode-electrolyte simulations:
boundary p p f    # non-periodic z
The z-direction has a vacuum gap. This creates two electrode surfaces exposed to vacuum (or vacuum region above electrolyte).
Problem with slab geometry: electrostatics in 2D is different from 3D. The naive Ewald/PPPM sum would include artificial dipole-dipole interactions between periodic images in z.
Why this matters: Without correction, the computed electrostatic energy depends on how many times you replicate the cell in z — clearly wrong for a single interface.
Solution: 2D Ewald / slab correction
kspace_modify slab 3
This applies a correction for the slab geometry: - Assumes the system is infinitely periodic in x, y - Assumes finite (non-periodic) in z - Adds a dipole correction term that accounts for the missing images
The number 3 refers to the dimensionality being treated as 2D (slab). LAMMPS automatically handles the correction.






WarningForgot kspace_modify slab?



If you use boundary p p f without kspace_modify slab, you will get: - Artificially high pressure in z-direction - Incorrect forces on atoms near the surface - Wrong double-layer structure and capacitance
Always add kspace_modify slab 3 (or equivalent) for non-periodic z.





The slab correction adds a term that accounts for the net dipole moment of the slab interacting with its periodic images. It has the form:
\[V_{dipole} = \frac{2\pi}{V} \left|\sum_i q_i z_i\right|^2\]
Where the sum is over all charges in the cell. This term is added to the reciprocal-space energy.
Physical interpretation: a polar slab has a dipole moment. In 3D periodic boundaries, that dipole would interact with infinitely many images. In slab geometry, only the x,y periodicity remains, and the correction accounts for the missing z-interactions.



boundary p p p    # fully periodic
# In fix electrode/conp:
fix fxconp bot electrode/conp -1.0 1.805 couple top 1.0 ffield on
With ffield on, the system is treated as an infinite stack of identical cells: - No vacuum region needed - Smaller z-dimension possible (saves atoms) - Requires symm on (total charge neutrality) - Uses internal E-field to apply potential difference: \(E = V/d\)
Advantages: - Better scaling for large systems (fully periodic) - No slab correction needed - Smaller cell means fewer atoms
Disadvantages: - Electrodes must be symmetric (infinite stack assumption) - Can’t model single-surface experiments - Requires careful treatment of dipole moment

title: Force Fields
text:
What Is a Force Field?
A force field is a set of mathematical functions and parameters that describe interatomic forces. It is an approximation — no force field is “correct”, only more or less appropriate for a given system and question.
The force field determines:

What interactions exist — which pairs have attractive/repulsive forces
How strong they are — the energy scale of binding
What is neglected — polarizability, electronic structure, chemical reactions


Force Field Components



Component
What It Describes
Typical Functional Form




Non-bonded
Van der Waals, electrostatics
LJ, Coulomb


Bonded
Chemical bonds
Harmonic, Morse


Angle
Three-body bending
Harmonic, cosine


Dihedral
Four-body torsion
Trigonometric series



For simple electrolytes (salt in water), only non-bonded interactions are needed. For explicit water models, bonds and angles are also required.

title: Force Fields
text:
Non-Bonded Interactions

Van der Waals (Dispersion/Repulsion)
The Lennard-Jones (LJ) potential is the workhorse of MD:
\[V(r) = 4\epsilon \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} - \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^6 \right]\]








Parameter
Physical Meaning
Typical Values (real units)




\(\epsilon\)
Depth of energy well (binding strength)
0.1–0.2 kcal/mol for atoms


\(\sigma\)
Distance where energy = zero
3.0–4.0 Å for light atoms




Term-by-Term Breakdown








Term
Physical Origin
Behavior




\(r^{-12}\)
Pauli exclusion (electron cloud repulsion)
Very steep; only matters at short range


\(r^{-6}\)
London dispersion (induced dipole attraction)
Softer; dominant at intermediate range



The r⁻¹² term is 4096× steeper than r⁻⁶ at r = σ. This is why LJ produces a hard-sphere-like repulsion at short distances while having a soft attractive well.
Why r⁻¹² specifically? It’s computationally convenient (easy to square), not because it represents any specific physical interaction. Other repulsion forms (Born-Mayer, exp) are more physically grounded but less common.


Visual Representation








Figure 1: Lennard-Jones potential: repulsion dominates at short range, attraction at intermediate range, zero at r=σ







Key Properties of LJ








Property
Value
Significance




Energy minimum
\(V_{min} = -\epsilon\) at \(r_{min} = 2^{1/6}\sigma \approx 1.12\sigma\)
Determines equilibrium spacing


Zero crossing
\(r = \sigma\)
Convenient reference point


Force zero
\(r = 2^{1/6}\sigma\)
Where attraction balances repulsion





LJ in LAMMPS
pair_style lj/cut 10.0    # LJ with cutoff at 10 Å
pair_coeff 1 1 0.15 3.5   # epsilon=0.15, sigma=3.5 (real units)
Cutoff considerations: - LJ is truncated at rcut — introduces error, but necessary for speed - Typical rcut = 10–12 Å for water; energy drift < 0.1% if cutoff is appropriate - Never exceed half the minimum box dimension — you would double-count interactions - Some use “shifted” LJ to make potential go smoothly to zero at cutoff: lammps   pair_style lj/cut/coul/long 10.0  # no shift   pair_style lj/charmm/coul/long 10.0 12.0  # with shift



Coulombic Electrostatics
\[V(r) = k \frac{q_1 q_2}{r}\]







Property
Value




Constant \(k\)
332.07 Å·kcal/mol·e² (real) or 14.3996 Å·eV·e² (metal)


Decay
\(r^{-1}\) — long-range, never truly zero


Energy scale
Much larger than LJ for charged systems



Why Coulomb is the hard problem: A pair of unit charges at 3 Å has \(V\) ≈ 110 kcal/mol (real units) — far larger than LJ well depths. And it doesn’t decay to zero at typical cutoffs.
This is why special methods (Ewald, PPPM) are needed — see ?@sec-electrostatics.

pair_coeff * * 0.15 3.5            # LJ for all pairs

kspace_style pppm 1e-5             # long-range solver (REQUIRED)
Key rule: If you use coul/long, you MUST use a kspace style like pppm or ewald. The long designation means “long-range handled by kspace”, not “I don’t need kspace”.

title: Force Fields
text:
Cross-Terms and Mixing Rules
When two different atom types interact, we need cross-pair parameters.

Lorentz-Berthelot Mixing
Default mixing rule in most force fields:
\[\epsilon_{ij} = \sqrt{\epsilon_{ii} \cdot \epsilon_{jj}}\] \[\sigma_{ij} = \frac{\sigma_{ii} + \sigma_{jj}}{2}\]
Physical meaning: - \(\sigma\) averaging = geometric mean of sizes (reasonable for van der Waals radii) - \(\epsilon\) averaging = arithmetic mean of energy depths
In LAMMPS, this is the default. If you specify only pair_coeff 1 1 and pair_coeff 2 2, the cross-term is computed automatically.


Explicit Cross-Parameters
Sometimes mixing rules give poor results. Override with explicit values:
pair_coeff 1 1 0.01 3.0    # type 1 - type 1
pair_coeff 2 2 0.05 3.5    # type 2 - type 2
pair_coeff 1 2 0.025 3.25  # type 1 - type 2 (explicit override)
When explicit is better: - Electrode-electrolyte interactions (metal-water cross terms often poorly described by mixing) - Systems with very different chemistries - When fitted to quantum calculations or experiment

title: Molecular Dynamics Fundamentals
text:
TipIn this section




What the simulation loop actually does and why it matters
How Newton’s laws connect to the trajectories MD produces
Key LAMMPS concepts mapped to physical meaning
How to read and interpret thermodynamic output
What the conserved quantity tells you about simulation quality





Molecular dynamics (MD) simulates atomic motion by solving Newton’s equations of motion numerically. At each timestep:

Forces are computed from atom positions using an interatomic potential (the force field)
Velocities and positions are updated via numerical integration

for timestep in range(N_steps):
    forces = compute_forces(positions, force_field)
    positions, velocities = integrate(positions, velocities, forces, dt)
The trajectory — the sequence of positions and velocities — is the primary output. From it, we compute thermodynamic properties by averaging over many timesteps.


For each of \(N\) atoms, we must compute: - Force from every other atom: \(O(N^2)\) interactions - With \(N = 10{,}000\) water molecules, that’s 100 million pair calculations per step - At 1 fs timestep, a 1 ns simulation needs 1 million steps
This is why long-range interactions (Coulomb) need special treatment (Ewald/PPPM) and why MD is routinely run on HPC clusters.



MD produces deterministic trajectories — given the same initial conditions, the same code produces identical results (in exact arithmetic). Real randomness comes from initial velocity sampling:
velocity all create 300.0 492845 rot yes mom yes
The 492845 is the random seed. Change it, get different initial velocities, same ensemble-averaged properties.






For each atom \(i\):
\[m_i \frac{d^2\mathbf{r}_i}{dt^2} = \mathbf{F}_i = -\nabla_i U(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{r}_N)\]
The force \(\mathbf{F}_i\) is the negative gradient of the potential energy \(U\) with respect to atom \(i\)’s position.



The standard integrator in LAMMPS is velocity Verlet:
# Step 1: Half-step velocity
v(t + Δt/2) = v(t) + 0.5 * F(t) / m * Δt

# Step 2: Full-step position
x(t + Δt) = x(t) + v(t + Δt/2) * Δt

# Step 3: Compute new forces at new positions
F(t + Δt) = -∇U(x(t + Δt))

# Step 4: Complete velocity
v(t + Δt) = v(t + Δt/2) + 0.5 * F(t + Δt) / m * Δt
Why this order? Because \(F(t + Δt)\) depends on \(x(t + Δt)\), which is only known after step 2.



The timestep \(\Delta t\) must be small enough to resolve the fastest motion in the system:



Motion
Period
Timestep Constraint




C-H bond stretch

title: Molecular Dynamics Fundamentals
text:
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulates atomic motion by solving Newton’s equations of motion numerically. At each timestep:

Forces are computed from atom positions using an interatomic potential (the force field)
Velocities and positions are updated via numerical integration

for timestep in range(N_steps):
    forces = compute_forces(positions, force_field)
    positions, velocities = integrate(positions, velocities, forces, dt)
The trajectory — the sequence of positions and velocities — is the primary output. From it, we compute thermodynamic properties by averaging over many timesteps.


For each of \(N\) atoms, we must compute: - Force from every other atom: \(O(N^2)\) interactions - With \(N = 10{,}000\) water molecules, that’s 100 million pair calculations per step - At 1 fs timestep, a 1 ns simulation needs 1 million steps
This is why long-range interactions (Coulomb) need special treatment (Ewald/PPPM) and why MD is routinely run on HPC clusters.



MD produces deterministic trajectories — given the same initial conditions, the same code produces identical results (in exact arithmetic). Real randomness comes from initial velocity sampling:
velocity all create 300.0 492845 rot yes mom yes
The 492845 is the random seed. Change it, get different initial velocities, same ensemble-averaged properties.

title: Molecular Dynamics Fundamentals
text:
For each atom \(i\):
\[m_i \frac{d^2\mathbf{r}_i}{dt^2} = \mathbf{F}_i = -\nabla_i U(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{r}_N)\]
The force \(\mathbf{F}_i\) is the negative gradient of the potential energy \(U\) with respect to atom \(i\)’s position.



The standard integrator in LAMMPS is velocity Verlet:
# Step 1: Half-step velocity
v(t + Δt/2) = v(t) + 0.5 * F(t) / m * Δt

# Step 2: Full-step position
x(t + Δt) = x(t) + v(t + Δt/2) * Δt

# Step 3: Compute new forces at new positions
F(t + Δt) = -∇U(x(t + Δt))

# Step 4: Complete velocity
v(t + Δt) = v(t + Δt/2) + 0.5 * F(t + Δt) / m * Δt
Why this order? Because \(F(t + Δt)\) depends on \(x(t + Δt)\), which is only known after step 2.

title: Constant Potential Molecular Dynamics in LAMMPS — Learning Taxonomy
text:
Introductory mechanics and electromagnetism (Coulomb’s law, electrostatic energy)
Basic chemistry (ions, water structure, what an electrode is)
One programming language (any) — for post-processing
No prior MD experience required





You have LAMMPS installed (or access to an HPC cluster with it)
You can run an input script and see log output
You want to understand what the commands mean, not just what they do





The goal is to connect LAMMPS input lines → physical meaning → simulation output
Theory sections explain the physics; Implementation sections show the corresponding LAMMPS syntax
Every major concept links to an observable you can measure









Newton determines atomic motion; forces come from interatomic potentials
A timestep Δt advances positions and velocities: x(t+Δt) = x(t) + v(t)Δt
Forces are recalculated at every step — this is what makes MD computationally expensive
The trajectory is a deterministic sequence; statistics over many steps give thermodynamic properties





Units — define the physical scale (real = Å, kcal/mol, fs; metal = Å, eV, ps). Mismatch causes garbage.
Atom style — what properties each particle carries. charge is mandatory for electrostatics.
Boundary — p p f means periodic in x,y, fixed (non-periodic) in z. Determines slab geometry for electrode simulations.
Pair styles — the functional form of the interatomic potential. Determines what forces exist.
Fixes — operations applied every timestep (integration, thermostats, constraints). The verb of LAMMPS.
Computes — calculate quantities on the fly (temperature, stress, charge density)
Groups — named subsets of atoms for targeted commands. Essential for distinguishing electrode from electrolyte.





Thermodynamic output — energy (total, kinetic, potential), temperature, pressure, volume
Energy conservation indicates a well-behaved simulation (NVE without thermostat)
Potential energy components (pair, bond, kspace) reveal where computation time goes
Drift in conserved quantity signals integration problems









A force field is a set of mathematical functions that describe interatomic forces
It is an approximation — no force field is “correct”, only appropriate for certain systems
Choice of force field determines what physics is captured (and what is omitted)
All force field parameters are fitted to experimental data or quantum calculations







Lennard-Jones (LJ): pair_style lj/cut — the workhorse of MD

Formula: V(r) = 4ε[(σ/r)^12 - (σ/r)^6]
ε = depth of the energy well (binding strength); σ = distance at which energy = zero
The r⁻¹² term is steep repulsion at short range; r⁻⁶ is softer attraction at longer range
Physical meaning: Pauli repulsion at short distance, induced-dipole attraction at longer range
Cutoff: LJ is truncated at some rcut — introduces error; rcut typically 10–12 Å for water
Why cut? Computation scales as N²; truncation saves time with acceptable error

Other forms: Buckingham, Morse, 12-6-4 (for metals), Gaussian — each suited to different materials





Formula: V(r) = k q₁q₂/r — long-range, never truly zero
The problem: Direct summation scales as N²; prohibitive for large systems
Solutions: Ewald summation, PPPM (Particle-Particle Particle-Mesh) — see Section 3





pair_style lj/cut/coul/long — LJ plus real-space Coulomb; k-space handles the long-range Coulomb
This is the standard choice for electrolyte simulations: LJ for repulsion/attraction, Coulomb for ionic interactions






Bonds: bond_style harmonic — spring-like; V = k(r - r₀)²

Water models (TIP3P, TIP4P) have explicit O-H bonds
Electrolyte ions may have internal bonds (e.g., carbonate)

Angles: angle between three atoms; important for water orientation
Dihedrals: rotations around bonds; relevant for organic electrolytes





Mixing rules: Lorentz-Berthelot (ε_ij = √(ε_i ε_j), σ_ij = (σ_i + σ_j)/2)
pair_coeff syntax: ID1 ID2 epsilon sigma for each unique pair type
All pairs must be defined: LAMMPS will error if any pair type is unspecified





Water models: TIP3P, TIP4P, SPC/E — each is a compromise between accuracy and cost
Ion parameters: from literature (e.g., Joung & Cheatham, 2008)
Electrode atoms: typically large ε for hard-wall repulsion, no Coulomb (metallic screening)
Physical meaning of LJ on electrodes: prevents electrolyte atoms from penetrating the surface; does not model bonding











Input
Output Effect

Potential energy scale; particle density; diffusion coefficient


dielectric
Strength of Coulomb interactions (vacuum = 1, water ≈ 80)


bond_style + bond_coeff
Vibrational spectra; bulk modulus; compressibility


Cutoff distance
Energy drift; simulation runtime (larger cut = slower but more accurate)











Real experiments control T, P (or V), and composition
In MD, we control what we simulate: NVE (microcanonical), NVT (canonical), NPT (isothermal-isobaric)
The choice is not just convention — it determines which statistical ensemble produces your output







Position update: x(t+Δt) = 2x(t) - x(t-Δt) + (F/m)Δt² (Verlet integration)
Velocity Verlet: v(t) = v(t-Δt) + 0.5(F(t) + F(t+Δt))Δt — more stable
Δt must be small enough to resolve the fastest motion (typically C-H bond vibration)
Typical values: Δt = 1 fs for explicit water; Δt = 0.5 fs if bonds are flexible; Δt = 2 fs with bond constraints





Too large Δt → energy drift, simulation “blows up” (atoms overlap catastrophically)
Too small Δt → wasted computation; results unchanged
Constraint: fix shake or fix rattle removes fast degrees of freedom, allowing larger Δt




fix 1 all nve          # basic NVE integration
fix 1 all nvt          # NVE + thermostat (see below)

nve = no thermostat; energy should be conserved (check E_total drift in log)
nvt = NVE modified by thermostat; total energy is NOT conserved








Temperature is a statistical property: T = (2/3Nk) × (1/2 mv²)_avg
Instantaneous T fluctuates; we average over time to compare to experiment
Thermostats manipulate velocities to sample the canonical ensemble

Kinetic energy → particle velocities → diffusion coefficient
Too high T → bond breaking, chemical reactions (LAMMPS not suited for this)
Too low T → slow dynamics, metastable states

Mechanical pressure from forces + kinetic contribution

Coulomb: V ∝ 1/r — long-range even at moderate distances
Direct summation: N(N-1)/2 pairs → computationally prohibitive for N > 1000
Periodic boundaries make the math non-trivial (Ewald, slab corrections)







Real space: short-range Coulomb interactions summed directly (cutoff-based)
Reciprocal space: long-range interactions handled via Fourier transform
Self term: corrects for double-counting of interactions in periodic systems





Controls the split between real and reciprocal space
Large α → narrow real-space Gaussian → faster real-space convergence → slower k-space
Small α → opposite
LAMMPS default is usually reasonable; for charged systems with small box, tuning may help








Ewald: O(N³/²) scaling — still bad for very large N
PPPM: maps charge to mesh, uses FFT → O(N log N)
Standard for systems with >10,000 atoms




kspace_style pppm 1e-5

1e-5 = desired RMS force accuracy (relative to force magnitude)
Tighter tolerance = more accurate but slower
For electrode systems: kspace_style pppm/electrode 1e-5






Small systems (N < 1000) or very short simulations: direct Coulomb with cutoff may suffice
pair_style coul/cut 10.0 — cutoff at 10 Å; no k-space calculation
Warning: ignoring long-range electrostatics introduces serious error; do not use for production







boundary p p f — z is non-periodic

A force field is a set of mathematical functions that describe interatomic forces
It is an approximation — no force field is “correct”, only appropriate for certain systems
Choice of force field determines what physics is captured (and what is omitted)
All force field parameters are fitted to experimental data or quantum calculations







Lennard-Jones (LJ): pair_style lj/cut — the workhorse of MD

Formula: V(r) = 4ε[(σ/r)^12 - (σ/r)^6]
ε = depth of the energy well (binding strength); σ = distance at which energy = zero
The r⁻¹² term is steep repulsion at short range; r⁻⁶ is softer attraction at longer range
Physical meaning: Pauli repulsion at short distance, induced-dipole attraction at longer range
Cutoff: LJ is truncated at some rcut — introduces error; rcut typically 10–12 Å for water
Why cut? Computation scales as N²; truncation saves time with acceptable error

Other forms: Buckingham, Morse, 12-6-4 (for metals), Gaussian — each suited to different materials





Formula: V(r) = k q₁q₂/r — long-range, never truly zero
The problem: Direct summation scales as N²; prohibitive for large systems
Solutions: Ewald summation, PPPM (Particle-Particle Particle-Mesh) — see Section 3

Electrolyte ions may have internal bonds (e.g., carbonate)

Angles: angle between three atoms; important for water orientation
Dihedrals: rotations around bonds; relevant for organic electrolytes

In MD, we control what we simulate: NVE (microcanonical), NVT (canonical), NPT (isothermal-isobaric)

Position update: x(t+Δt) = 2x(t) - x(t-Δt) + (F/m)Δt² (Verlet integration)
Velocity Verlet: v(t) = v(t-Δt) + 0.5(F(t) + F(t+Δt))Δt — more stable
Δt must be small enough to resolve the fastest motion (typically C-H bond vibration)
Typical values: Δt = 1 fs for explicit water; Δt = 0.5 fs if bonds are flexible; Δt = 2 fs with bond constraints

text:
This guide teaches you to run constant potential molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using the LAMMPS ELECTRODE package. It is written for researchers and students who have access to a working LAMMPS installation and want to understand the physics behind the commands — not just the syntax.
By “physics” we mean: - What does a Lennard-Jones potential actually describe? - Why does controlling temperature require a thermostat, and how do different thermostats work? - What does constant potential mean for an electrode, and why is it different from constant charge? - How does the capacitance matrix emerge from electrostatics?

Real experiments control temperature, pressure, and composition. In MD, we choose which of these to hold fixed — this determines the statistical ensemble and thus which thermodynamic properties we can legitimately compute.

The ensemble choice is not just convention — it determines which statistical mechanics formula you must use to connect simulation results to experimental observables.
Example: If you run NVT and compute the compressibility, you need to use the NVT formula for fluctuations, not the NPT formula. Using the wrong ensemble = wrong physics.





In MD, temperature is defined from kinetic energy:

title: Electrodes and the Constant Potential Method
text:
TipIn this section




Why conductors need different treatment than insulators in MD
What the constant potential method does and why it matters for electrochemistry
How induced charges emerge from constrained energy minimization
The capacitance matrix and what it tells you about your system
Comparison with other polarizable methods







In a typical molecular simulation (water, proteins, simple electrolytes):

Atomic charges are fixed at their initial values
The electrostatic potential within the material varies freely depending on charge distribution
No charge redistribution occurs during the simulation

This is appropriate for insulators, where charges cannot move through the material.



In a metal (electrode):

Charges (electrons) can move freely within the material
The material adjusts its charge distribution to equalize the electrostatic potential
This happens on timescales much faster than atomic motion (effectively instantaneous)

If we treat a metal electrode with fixed charges, we’re getting the physics wrong — the electrode cannot maintain arbitrary charge distributions.
The key difference: In a conductor, the electrostatic potential is the same throughout the material. In an insulator, charges are fixed and potentials can vary.






When an electrode is placed in electrolyte:

Electric double layer: ions accumulate near the charged surface
Solvation shells: water molecules orient near the surface
Applied potential: changing the electrode voltage changes ion adsorption

The structure of the double layer determines the capacitance — a key measurable quantity in electrochemistry.



In real electrochemistry, the potential (voltage) of the electrode is the controlled variable, measured and maintained by a potentiostat.
In a typical MD simulation with fixed atom charges, we can only control the total charge on the electrode — not the potential. This is wrong for electrochemistry.









Controlled Variable
Physical Reality
Fixed-Charge MD
Constant Potential




Electrode potential
What the potentiostat controls
❌ Cannot enforce
✅ Direct control


Electrode charge
Flows from potential
✅ Can set
❌ Fluctuates






Consider a simulation of charging a supercapacitor:

We start with neutral electrodes
We want to apply 1 V between electrodes
With fixed charges: we must choose some total charge on each electrode — but what charge gives 1 V?
The relationship between charge and potential depends on the electrolyte structure (which we don’t know a priori)

With constant potential, the charges emerge from the physics — we specify the voltage and the simulation determines the induced charge.
Example: The same 1 V applied across: - Vacuum → no charge flows (capacitance ~0) - Ionic liquid → large induced charge (high capacitance) - Aqueous salt → moderate charge (intermediate capacitance)
The capacitance depends on the electrolyte. Fixed charge can’t capture this.






We have a system with: - Electrode atoms with unknown charges \(q_i\) (to be determined) - Electrolyte atoms with known charges \(Q_j\) (fixed) - A constraint: each electrode surface must be at potential \(V\)
The electrostatic energy in matrix form:
\[E(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{Q}) = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{q}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{q} + \mathbf{q}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{Q} + \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{Q}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{Q}\]
Where \(\mathbf{A}\) is the inverse capacitance matrix (from the kspace solver). This comes from solving Poisson’s equation with the system geometry.
We want to minimize \(E\) subject to the constraint that each electrode group is at target potential \(V_k\).



The mathematical approach uses Lagrange multipliers. We minimize:
\[\mathcal{L} = E(\mathbf{q}) + \sum_k \lambda_k (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q})_k - V_k\]
Where \(\lambda_k\) are Lagrange multipliers enforcing \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}\).
Taking \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{q} = 0\):
\[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q} + \mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q} + \mathbf{A}^T \boldsymbol{\lambda} = 0\]
But this simplifies: the constraint is \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}\), so \(\boldsymbol{\lambda} = \mathbf{V}\) and we get:
\[\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}(\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q})\]
The matrix \(\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \mathbf{C}\) is the capacitance matrix. The induced electrode charges depend on: - The applied potential \(\mathbf{V}\) - The electrolyte configuration \(\mathbf{Q}\) (through the \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q}\) term) - The geometric capacitance \(\mathbf{C}\)



The N×N capacitance matrix \(\mathbf{C}\) relates electrode potentials to electrode charges:
\[\mathbf{Q}_{electrode} = \mathbf{C} \cdot \mathbf{V}\]
But for systems with electrolyte present, there’s also a zero-voltage contribution:
\[\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{Q}_{0V} + \mathbf{C} \cdot \mathbf{V}\]







Symbol
Meaning




\(\mathbf{Q}\)
Total charge on each electrode group


\(\mathbf{Q}_{0V}\)
Charge configuration at zero applied potential (influenced by electrolyte structure)


\(\mathbf{C}\)
Capacitance matrix; depends only on geometry and dielectric


\(\mathbf{V}\)
Applied potentials on each electrode group



Physical meaning of \(C_{ij}\): How much charge on electrode \(i\) changes when electrode \(j\)’s potential changes, with all other potentials held constant.
For a symmetric two-electrode capacitor: - \(C_{11} = C_{22}\) (diagonal elements) - \(C_{12} = C_{21}\) (off-diagonal; negative — raising \(V_1\) induces opposite charge on electrode 2)
What you can compute from C: - Total capacitance: \(C_{total} = \sum_{i,j} C_{ij}\) - Differential capacitance: \(dQ/dV\) at given V - Potential distribution in complex geometries - Response to potential sweep (cyclic voltammetry-like)



Point charges at the electrode surface create a singularity — as an electrolyte ion approaches the surface, the interaction energy diverges (Coulomb catastrophe). This makes the matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) ill-conditioned and difficult to invert.
The solution: Smear each electrode charge over a Gaussian distribution:
\[\rho_i(\mathbf{r}) = q_i \left(\frac{\eta_i}{\pi}\right)^{3/2} \exp(-\eta_i |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{R}_i|^2)\]
The smearing width η (eta) controls:







η (large)
η (small)




Narrow distribution (more like point charge)
Wide distribution (smoother, better conditioned)


More accurate electrostatics near surface
Better matrix convergence; smoother potential


Harder to converge (singular matrix)
Easier to solve



Typical η ≈ 1.0–2.0 Å⁻¹ (real units) or 0.2–0.5 (metal units).
Physical interpretation: Smearing mimics the fact that real metals have a finite electron density at the surface — the charges are not point-like. The Gaussian width parameter should be chosen to match the electron gas density of the electrode material.












Aspect
Constant Potential (electrode/conp)
Constant Charge (electrode/conq)




What is fixed
Voltage on each electrode group
Total charge on each electrode group


What fluctuates
Electrode atom charges
Electrode potentials


Physical analog
Potentiostat
Galvanostat


Use case
Electrochemical experiments
Battery discharge (known charge flux)


Output
Induced charges
Measured potentials


Advantage
Direct comparison to experiment
Models known current


Disadvantage
Charge can spike during fast dynamics
Potential response may be unexpected





Constant potential (electrode/conp): - Comparing to electrochemical experiments (CV, EIS) - Studying double-layer structure at controlled voltage - Capacitance measurements - Modeling supercapacitors or electrochemical capacitors
Constant charge (electrode/conq): - Modeling battery cycling (known current → known charge change) - When you know the amount of charge injected/extracted - Studying potential response to charging/discharging - Simulating galvanostatic experiments






The electric double layer has characteristic regions:

Inner layer (Helmholtz): specifically adsorbed ions, water molecules. Distance ~0.3–0.5 nm from surface.
Outer layer (Helmholtz): solvated ions attracted by coulomb but not specifically adsorbed. Distance ~0.5–1 nm.
Diffuse layer: decaying ion concentration into bulk. Distance ~1–10 nm depending on ionic strength.

CPM captures all of these — ion density profiles near electrodes reflect the balance of electrostatic attraction and ionic excluded-volume effects.



Water molecules near electrodes: - Orient with H atoms toward negative electrode, O toward positive - Form layers (oscillating density) near the surface - This structure affects capacitance (Frumkin correction)
The force field (water model) determines how realistic this structure is. Different water models (SPC/E, TIP4P) give different capacitances.











Parameter
Effect on Capacitance
Physical Reason




Ion size
Larger ions → lower capacitance
Excluded volume reduces available space


Ion charge
Higher charge → stronger adsorption
Different capacitance peak position


Electrode structure
Sharp features → field enhancement
Higher local capacitance at tips/edges


Water model dielectric
Higher ε → higher capacitance
Better screening reduces electrostatic penalty


Temperature
Higher T → lower capacitance
Thermal disruption of ordered structure


Potential
Non-linear C(V)
Double layer saturation at high V
















Method
What It Does
When to Use
How CPM Differs




Drude oscillators
Adds extra particle to model electron cloud polarizability
Metals, polarizable anions
CPM controls boundary potential, not internal polarizability


Core-shell
Adds massless shell for ionic polarizability
Polarizable ions (Ca²⁺)
CPM is for electrode boundaries


QEq (charge equilibration)
Redistributes charges within a single molecule based on electronegativity
Organic molecules, chemical reactions
CPM handles electrode-electrolyte boundary


Fixed charge
No polarizability
Insulators, vacuum
Wrong for metals





CPM is a classical method. It does not compute electronic structure. For:








Level
Method
What It Gives




Classical MD
CPM
Electrode charges, double layer structure


DFTB
DFT-based tight binding
Electronic structure at interface


QM/MM
Quantum region + classical MM
Accurate reaction at electrode


CPMD
Car-Parrinello MD
Full electronic structure (expensive)



CPM assumptions: - Electrode charges respond instantly to electrostatic environment (adiabatic) - Metal is treated as a perfect conductor (except for smearing parameter) - No chemical bonding between electrode and electrolyte
When CPM may fail: - Charge transfer across interface (faradaic currents) - Chemical reactions at electrode surface - Very sharp tips where quantum tunneling matters - Highlycorrelated electrolytes (ionic liquids at high charge)

Complete working script you can adapt for your system





A planar electrode supercapacitor with: - Two gold electrodes (top and bottom) - SPC/E water with 1M NaCl electrolyte - Constant potential mode (1 V difference) - NVT ensemble at 300 K
Goal: By the end, you should understand every line of this input and know how to modify it for your own system.



units metal
atom_style charge
boundary p p f
Physical meaning:








Command
Physical Meaning
Why




units metal
Å, eV, ps
Standard for materials; electrode parameters usually in eV


atom_style charge
Each atom has charge
Required for electrostatics; no bonds needed for simple electrolytes


boundary p p f
Slab geometry
Two electrode surfaces; vacuum region above electrolyte



Why not units real? Many electrode force field parameters are published in eV (metal units). Using units real would require converting kcal/mol to eV (factor of 23.06). If your parameters are in kcal/mol, use units real.



variable Lx equal 20
variable Ly equal 20
variable Lz equal 60

region box block 0 $Lx 0 $Ly 0 $Lz
create_box 5 box    # 1=bot electrode, 2=top, 3=O, 4=H, 5=Na, 6=Cl
Box dimensions: 20×20×60 Å = 24,000 Å³ For water at 1 g/cm³, this holds ~480 water molecules (the electrolyte region is 20×20×50 Å = 20,000 Å³).
# Define regions
region bot block 0 $Lx 0 $Ly 0 5
region top block 0 $Lx 0 $Ly 55 $Lz
region elyte block 0 $Lx 0 $Ly 5 55

# Create atoms
create_atoms 1 region bot    # bottom electrode (type 1)
create_atoms 2 region top    # top electrode (type 2)
# Water and ions: use moltemplate, packmol, or convert from structure file
Physical meaning of regions:









Region
Size
Purpose
Atom Count (estimate)




box
20×20×60 Å
Full simulation cell
—


bot
20×20×5 Å
Bottom electrode
~200 Au atoms


top
20×20×5 Å
Top electrode
~200 Au atoms


elyte
20×20×50 Å
Water + ions between
~480 water + 10 Na + 10 Cl



Why 50 Å gap? The electrode separation should be large enough that periodic images in x,y don’t interact through the electrolyte. For 1M salt, Debye length ≈ 10 Å, so 50 Å is sufficient.
# Define groups
group bot region bot
group top region top
group elyte region elyte
group electrode union bot top
group mobile subtract all electrode    # electrolyte only



pair_style lj/cut/coul/long 10.0
Why lj/cut/coul/long? We need: - LJ for short-range repulsion/attraction - Coulomb for ionic interactions - long suffix = long-range handled by kspace (pppm/electrode)


# Electrode-electrode (soft repulsion, no chemical bonding)
pair_coeff 1 1 0.01 3.0    # ε=0.01 eV, σ=3.0 Å (soft repulsion)
pair_coeff 2 2 0.01 3.0    # same for top
pair_coeff 1 2 0.005 3.0   # cross-term (smaller)
Why ε=0.01 eV? This is a soft repulsion that prevents electrolyte atoms from penetrating the electrode. Real metallic bonding is much stronger but is not modeled (CPM handles charge response instead).
Why σ=3.0 Å? Approximately matches Au atomic radius. The electrode atoms are just “soft spheres” preventing overlap.



# Water LJ (SPC/E)
pair_coeff 3 3 0.155 3.166    # O: ε=0.155 eV, σ=3.166 Å
pair_coeff 4 4 0.0 0.0        # H: no LJ (charged but no van der Waals)

# Ion LJ (Joung & Cheatham for SPC/E)
pair_coeff 5 5 0.0874 3.40    # Na: ε=0.0874 eV, σ=3.40 Å
pair_coeff 6 6 0.100 4.45      # Cl: ε=0.100 eV, σ=4.45 Å



# Electrode-water
pair_coeff 1 3 0.005 3.1    # bot-O: mixed using Lorentz-Berthelot
pair_coeff 2 3 0.005 3.1    # top-O: same
pair_coeff 1 4 0.0 0.0      # bot-H: no LJ
pair_coeff 2 4 0.0 0.0      # top-H: no LJ

# Ion-water (important for solvation)
pair_coeff 5 3 0.114 3.28    # Na-O
pair_coeff 6 3 0.124 3.81    # Cl-O
pair_coeff 5 4 0.0 0.0       # Na-H: no LJ
pair_coeff 6 4 0.0 0.0       # Cl-H: no LJ

# Ion-electrode
pair_coeff 1 5 0.005 3.2    # bot-Na
pair_coeff 2 5 0.005 3.2    # top-Na
pair_coeff 1 6 0.005 3.7    # bot-Cl
pair_coeff 2 6 0.005 3.7    # top-Cl

# Ion-ion
pair_coeff 5 6 0.0935 3.925  # Na-Cl (Lorentz-Berthelot)

All unique atom type pairs must be defined. LAMMPS will error if any pair is missing. Use * for wildcards: pair_coeff * 4 0.0 0.0 means “all types with type 4 have zero LJ”.

kspace_modify slab 3
Why pppm/electrode? Standard pppm doesn’t provide the electrode-electrode interaction matrix that ELECTRODE needs.
Why slab 3? Non-periodic z requires the 2D Ewald correction. The 3 means the third dimension (z) is non-periodic.

Value
Meaning

1.805

pair_style lj/cut/coul/long 10.0
Why lj/cut/coul/long? We need: - LJ for short-range repulsion/attraction - Coulomb for ionic interactions - long suffix = long-range handled by kspace (pppm/electrode)


# Electrode-electrode (soft repulsion, no chemical bonding)
pair_coeff 1 1 0.01 3.0    # ε=0.01 eV, σ=3.0 Å (soft repulsion)
pair_coeff 2 2 0.01 3.0    # same for top
pair_coeff 1 2 0.005 3.0   # cross-term (smaller)
Why ε=0.01 eV? This is a soft repulsion that prevents electrolyte atoms from penetrating the electrode. Real metallic bonding is much stronger but is not modeled (CPM handles charge response instead).
Why σ=3.0 Å? Approximately matches Au atomic radius. The electrode atoms are just “soft spheres” preventing overlap.



# Water LJ (SPC/E)
pair_coeff 3 3 0.155 3.166    # O: ε=0.155 eV, σ=3.166 Å
pair_coeff 4 4 0.0 0.0        # H: no LJ (charged but no van der Waals)

pair_coeff 5 5 0.0874 3.40    # Na: ε=0.0874 eV, σ=3.40 Å
pair_coeff 6 6 0.100 4.45      # Cl: ε=0.100 eV, σ=4.45 Å

pair_coeff 6 3 0.124 3.81    # Cl-O

pair_coeff 6 4 0.0 0.0       # Cl-H: no LJ

# Ion-electrode
pair_coeff 1 5 0.005 3.2    # bot-Na
pair_coeff 2 5 0.005 3.2    # top-Na
pair_coeff 1 6 0.005 3.7    # bot-Cl
pair_coeff 2 6 0.005 3.7    # top-Cl

pair_coeff 5 6 0.0935 3.925  # Na-Cl (Lorentz-Berthelot)

All unique atom type pairs must be defined. LAMMPS will error if any pair is missing. Use * for wildcards: pair_coeff * 4 0.0 0.0 means “all types with type 4 have zero LJ”.

Why pppm/electrode? Standard pppm doesn’t provide the electrode-electrode interaction matrix that ELECTRODE needs.
Why slab 3? Non-periodic z requires the 2D Ewald correction. The 3 means the third dimension (z) is non-periodic.
